In response to the current trend of decentralization between the central and local levels, the People's Republic of China promulgated the Local Institutions Act on January 25th,88, which combines the rules governing the separation of municipalities and municipalities, and opens a new page on the history of local self-government development in Taiwan.
The Taipei Council is a local legislative body that monitors the municipalities on behalf of the citizens, and the legislative power is exercised by members of each district representing a pluralistic society.

In 1998, the Taipei city government registered it as a city monument, so in order to keep the building for longer periods of time, it worked in partnership with the public and private sectors. Construction rehabilitation works began in 2002 for a period of five years.
In 2008, cultural promotion was re-established in the form of a re-establishment of the 100-year-old house, which is an important example of the preservation of Taiwan's cultural assets.
There are currently over 5,000 items in the museum, ranging from the history of local hot springs (such as pottery in the north, hotel books, leaf drawings) to the ceremonial objects of life of the Han people, the fabrics of the indigenous people, carvings, embroidery, and the richness of the multicultural mix.

The foundation is in Lanyang Creek, where people grow up in the middle of the year, and as they develop, they grow into communities, with crossing points, and become important waterways to communicate with the plains of the Sun.
From the early rice-farming industry to the paper industry developed during the Japanese regime, the community has developed a concentration of paper-based industries;
In addition, the temples in the community are at the heart of the faith and are known for its unique "overfire" ritual.
Rice culture is home to rice production in the Lanyang plains from ancient times, and the "two-block barn" near the station was responsible for buying and transferring rice from the vast agricultural areas.
The building witnessed the booming rice industry and the development of the local economy at the time, and despite the fact that it has entered history with the changing times, the second barn has drawn attention to its elegant and pristine look.
At present, the building has been made an ancient county and has been converted into an exhibition of rice culture, allowing tourists to learn about rice cultivation and the daily lives of rice farmers.
In addition, Shenzhen was once the lifeline of the local farming industry and remains an important testimony to the rice culture.
The second and fourth regions of paper culture originated in the era of Japanese treatment, when a paper factory was set up near the sugar mill to make the paper by using the remaining sugar cane slag from sugar.
China's paper industry, which used to be one of the largest news-based paper-producing industries in the country, has so far brought economic and cultural dynamism to the region, despite the fact that two and four paper-producing areas have ceased to operate.
The paper factory's chimneys were a symbol of the return of tourists and a reminder of the industrial development of the land.
In addition, the development of the paper mills has led to a change in the whole type of life in the community.
The second royal temple of religious culture has been an important religious centre for the community since the beginning of the 51st year.
The King, the Three Kings, is a local god from Fujian Yi Po, who died in the last year of his struggle against Mongolia.
His powers are closely related to medicine, imams, and the law enforcement system, which provide medical care, disaster relief and demon removal services to immigrants in the process of development, and serve as a spiritual pillar of the population.
The special rituals of the Second King's temple, such as the "Wu Guang Yi" and "overfire", have become known religious cultures throughout the station and have attracted the participation of followers from across the country.
The history of the King's excesses dates back to more than a hundred years and was elected as one of Taiwan's religious sites in 96, demonstrating its profound influence in local culture.

Attractions.Description:
The old tea factory was founded in 1956 (45 years), while the tea factory was built in 1959 (48 years).
During the Japanese regime, the Taiwan Governor General's Office developed the tea industry, especially the fishing ponds around the sunset as a red tea production site, where the climate is warm and fertile.
When the tea factory was set up, it was introduced with the most advanced equipment, which led to the introduction of the British red tea industry, thus laying an important foundation for the sale of Taiwan red tea.
In the post-war period, the tea factory continued to play an important role in Taiwan's red tea outlet, creating new high prices and showing a boom.
After the major earthquake of 921 in 1999, which hit the south, the sun and the old tea mills responded positively to the "one country, one country, one country, one country, one country, one country, one country, one country, one country, another country, another country, another country, another country, another country, and another country.
The use of agropharmaceuticals began in 2003 and was further transformed into a tourist factory in 2008.
Today's tea factory is managed by friendly farming and organic farming, mainly producing tea varieties such as 8 (Assam), 18 (Red Jade) and 21 (Red Sing).
In the decade since the earthquake, the tea factory has been working to promote the tea industry in the fish pool, not only to guide small farmers and entrepreneurs around, to pass on tea technology, but also to assist industry workers, and to boost the multi-dimensional development of the south, thereby injecting new life into the tea industry.
In terms of building features, the tea factory has been crafted to integrate Japanese-style construction styles and Taiwan's local construction materials.
The design of the building blocks that bind together the walls of the red bricks not only takes into account the actual need for ventilated heat, but also adds to the excellent construction.
High tea spaces and unique ventilation designs preserve the building features of the early tea industry.
There are many valuable tea facilities in the factory, such as fermentation machines, fermentation beds, which are important not only for industrial heritage, but also for evidence of the development of the tea industry in Taiwan, through which we can see early tea production processes and the lives of workers.
The tea factory has always been close to the tea farmers around it, and is a valuable memory shared by the local population.
Many old tea farmers are still able to tell the story of the tea harvest and the drops of the tea made in that year, and these precious oral histories have added to the story of the tea factory.
Over time, the old tea factory has been transformed into a cultural park, and while preserving the traditional culture of tea production, it also actively integrates modern creative elements to demonstrate the new value of cultural assets in the industry.
Through a variety of exhibitions and experiences, the tea factory continues to convey the unique charms of Taiwan’s tea culture to the public.
There are still large green tea gardens around the tea factory, and the sun is shining with the sun and the sun, creating a unique cultural landscape that not only bears witness to the development of the tea industry in Taiwan, but also a valuable cultural landscape.

Attractions.Description:
New North City's central city of Hua Xinxin Street, or Myanmar Street, is one of the areas of Taiwan where Filipino immigrants are concentrated.
The neighborhood is not only a place of life and residence for Myanmar immigrants, but also a story of the diaspora fighting in Taiwan and trying to integrate into Taiwan society.
The cultural characteristics of the New Street, not only in the daily lives of the shop, signboards, family members, but also the temples that are hidden in the streets, fully reflect the troubled situation in Myanmar, where Myanmar immigrants have fled for generations and have come to seek their lives, gather community awareness and rebuild their new homes in the diaspora.
The move was a bet my name is Yang Wanli, born in Burma, from Yunnan, who has eight children in his seventh row.
After a long period of social unrest, which was detrimental to the long run, the entire family began to draw up a plan for his migration, which began in 1984, when they moved with their children to Taiwan to seek peace, moving their homes many times, and finally ending up on China City.
And it took 10 years to complete the journey.
And this one is 30 more.
Parents, like other residents of Washington, D.C., are Myanmar immigrants who share their lives in Taiwan, from work sites to factories, and who do all kinds of work, but the only thing remains that they have never left New China.
In the long run, as in the case of other immigrants, the elders of the street have already determined that this block, less than 500 metres, is their home.
Taiwan has long been their homeland.
Plurality: Every day in the neighborhood, when they get a chance to walk into New York City, when the smell of tea and rich spices comes out of their noses, they can feel a strong foreign feeling.
Not only is it possible to see the Chinese sign in the streets, but it is also a multicultural phenomenon that has emerged from a combination of ethnic groups, including Myanmar, Yunnan, Thailand, and even India, which is increasingly attracting tourists from Taiwan to the pilgrimage and is therefore declared a South China View Food Street.
However, this block does not exist solely for tourists, and more importantly, it is also a place of daily life for Filipino immigrants, where multiculturalism is not a slogan, but a daily one.
Every morning, the southern Buddhist monks, dressed in red red, walk barefoot on the streets of Hua Xinjiang, and the inhabitants straddle and esteemfully feed all kinds of food, creating a special cultural landscape for each morning.
In midlife, I decided to stand up for the 10-year-olds who came to Taiwan with their parents, to enter elementary school in China City, where classes are not kept up, words are spoken, and food is always the same as class, and where group life is always unattractive, difficult to adapt to, and often called "Myanmars."
Mom and Dad always told me to swallow it up, and I didn't understand it when I was a kid, but when I grew up, I learned that the Filipino immigrant generation had come to Taiwan to look for a "home" where their children could live and be educated.
I want to be able to stand up for the streets with the concept of a cultural bridge, and I want our life stories to be told, recorded and remembered.

Attractions.Description:
The first modern industrial complex in Taiwan was established in 1901 at the Takahashi Bridge.
In 2001, a group of artists, together with the Hibashi organization, converted the historic industrial site into a cultural preservation cluster and launched the first phase of the Artistic Village of the Hashibashi.
In 2008, the Artists' Village Settlement Project began to be run jointly by Bridge Head White House Inc. and the Taiwan Arts Development Association, renting space for former guesthouses and warehouses from the Taiwan Sugar Corporation, mainly in the areas of cultural assets, environmental education, common aesthetics, art collections, and fully self-financing projects to promote artists' village presence.
This is not just an artist's room and studio, but also a quarterly event on different topics.
The Bridge Head Sugar Factory, which ceased to make sugar in 1997, was declared an ancient county by the Governor of Takao County in 2002 and its former antiquities, such as sugar mills, Japanese wooden dormitories, bomb shelters, red brick towers, 100-year-old trees, etc., were preserved.
The sugar factory itself is still run by Taiwan Sugar Corporation, but has been transformed into a no-go-seeing industry, now being built as a Taiwan Sugar Museum.
Sugar mills are fast-forwarded, with tourist traffic on holiday, becoming an important tourist attraction in southern Taiwan and attracting a significant number of tourists.
In 2008, the spirit of the Bridge Head Village of Art, which was set up by civil society organizations, continued to invite artists to sugar factories to engage in creative and environmental conversations, more indicative of future developments in the arts industry or cultural parks.
